events.title: McCarthy v. Hernandez: SCOTUS reverses Second Circuit habeas grant on Miranda/Seibert jury instruction issue
events.summary: The Supreme Court reversed a Second Circuit decision that had granted habeas relief to Pedro Hernandez, a state prisoner convicted of murder in New York. The Second Circuit had held that federal law (specifically Justice Kennedy's concurrence in Missouri v. Seibert) required the trial court to instruct the jury on the "attenuation" doctrine when the jury asked whether an initial pre-Miranda confession tainted later post-Miranda confessions. SCOTUS held that Seibert addressed only judicial suppression motions, not jury deliberations, and that no clearly established federal law required such a jury instruction. The Court vacated and reversed, reinstating Hernandez's conviction.
events.why_relevant: This decision narrows federal habeas review and restricts the scope of Miranda protections by holding that trial courts need not instruct juries on attenuation doctrine, even when juries explicitly ask about it.
events.basis: No clearly established federal law required the trial court to instruct the jury about the rule that Justice Kennedy adopted in Seibert. Because the panel erred in holding otherwise, we grant the State's petition for a writ of certiorari, reverse the judgment of the Second Circuit, and remand the case for further proceedings consistent with this opinion.

events.title: Summary judgment ruling — Pablo Sequen v. Albarran (N.D. Cal.) 5:25-cv-06487
events.summary: Judge Pitts granted Plaintiffs' motion for final class certification of the provisionally certified courthouse-arrest class and the detention class, and granted Plaintiffs' motions for partial summary judgment on their Administrative Procedure Act (APA) claims. The court vacated ICE's 2025 courthouse-arrest policies (ICE Policy Nos. 11072.3 and 11072.4) and Executive Office for Immigration and Review's (EOIR) 2025 courthouse-arrest policy (OPPM 25-06) as arbitrary and capricious. The court found that ICE's 2025 policies rescinded the agency's 2021 guidance - which had restricted courthouse arrests at immigration courts - without acknowledging that change, providing any substitute guidance for immigration courthouses, or addressing the chilling effects on hearing attendance that had motivated the prior policy. Further, the court found that EOIR's policy rested on the false premise that ICE had validly rescinded its 2021 guidance, failed to recognize that EOIR retained discretion to mirror ICE's 2025 limits rather than eliminate all restrictions, and provided no rational explanation for rejecting the 2023 guidance's core concern that courthouse arrests would deter noncitizen attendance at removal proceedings. The court also vacated ICE's June 24, 2025 Nationwide Hold Room Waiver (extending hold-room detention from 12 to 72 hours) as arbitrary and capricious, finding that ICE failed to consider alternatives, created an internal inconsistency with existing detention standards, and did not consider its constitutional obligation to avoid punitive conditions of civil confinement. The court ordered nationwide vacatur rather than the class-limited injunction the government sought, holding that APA § 706's instruction to “set aside” arbitrary agency action requires vacatur of the policies themselves and that Trump v. CASA (2025) - which limited universal injunctions under the Judiciary Act of 1789 - explicitly does not address APA vacatur. The court also rejected the government's argument that § 1252(f)(1) barred a nationwide vacatur, holding that APA vacatur operates on the policy rather than on the parties and therefore does not constitute “injunctive relief” within statute § 1252(f)(1)'s prohibition. On the detention conditions claims, the court separately rejected the government's contention that detainees' varying statutory bases for detention precluded class-wide relief, holding that substantive due process rights concerning physical conditions of confinement do not vary by statute.

events.title: Summary judgment ruling — State of California v. Trump (D. Mass.) 1:25-cv-10810
events.summary: Judge Casper granted in part Plaintiff States' motion for partial summary judgment and granted in part the executive branch's cross-motion, permanently enjoining Defendants from implementing or enforcing §§ 2(a), 3(d), 4(a), 7(a) and 7(b) of Executive Order 14248. The court determined that §§ 2(a) and 3(d) - which require citizenship proof for federal voter registration - are ultra vires and unconstitutionally violate the separation of powers. Further, the court found § 2(a) to be inconsistent with the National Voter Registration Act (NVRA), and § 3(d) with the Uniformed and Overseas Absentee Voting Act (UOCAVA), respectively. The court permanently enjoined enforcement of §§ 2(a) and 3(d) nationwide. The court granted Plaintiff States relief against § 4(a), which cuts off federal funding from the Election Assistance Commission (EAC) to states that fail to comply with the citizenship proof requirement - except as to Wisconsin, which it denied on standing grounds. The court agreed with Plaintiff States that the Attorney General had no legal basis to sue any state that counted mail-in ballots received after Election Day under § 7(a) of the EO. The court blocked § 7(a) only as to the 13 Ballot Receipt States. The non-Ballot Receipt States' claims against § 7(a) was dismissed on standing grounds, as those states have no late-ballot laws to protect from the EO. The court also blocked § 7(b) as to the Ballot Receipt States. The court did not fully resolve the non-Ballot Receipt States' challenge to § 7(b), which directs the EAC to cut off funding for states that count mail-in ballots received after Election Day. The court declined to resolve the non-Ballot Receipt States' § 7(b) claim, requesting both sides to report back by July 10, 2026 as to whether the non-Ballot Receipt Plaintiff States will still pursue that claim.

events.title: Historical commemoration of the 150th anniversary of the Battle of the Little Bighorn
events.summary: The article marks the 150th anniversary of the Battle of the Little Bighorn on June 25, 1876, when Lakota warriors defeated Lieutenant Colonel George Armstrong Custer's 7th Cavalry. The essay provides historical context tracing the conflict from the 1862 Dakota War through the 1868 Fort Laramie Treaty, which guaranteed the Great Sioux Reservation to the Lakota. It describes how gold discoveries in the Black Hills, prospector incursions, and the U.S. government's failed attempt to purchase the sacred land led to military escalation and ultimately Custer's defeat.
events.why_relevant: The article examines how broken treaties, government coercion, and military aggression against Indigenous peoples shaped American history and democratic accountability for state violence.
events.basis: Today marks the 150th anniversary of the Battle of the Little Bighorn in 1876, when Lieutenant Colonel George Armstrong Custer, who led the 7th Cavalry, lost his entire command to Lakota warriors.

events.title: University of Kentucky study documents immune system changes in East Palestine train disaster residents
events.summary: Researchers published a peer-reviewed pilot study examining blood samples from residents of East Palestine, Ohio, who were exposed to toxic chemical releases from a Norfolk Southern train derailment in February 2023. The study found that exposed residents showed elevated red blood cells, hemoglobin, inflammation markers, and immune-response proteins six months after the accident, suggesting their bodies were still fighting chemical exposure. The research will expand to a larger cohort of residents and first responders.
events.why_relevant: The study documents long-term health damage from a major industrial disaster and raises questions about the adequacy of government evacuation and air-monitoring protocols in protecting public health.

events.title: Trump administration shut down criminal investigation into clemency
events.summary: The New York Times reported that the Trump administration terminated a criminal investigation into Trump's December 2025 commutation of David Gentile, a private equity executive convicted of securities and wire fraud in a $1.6 billion scheme. Investigators had discovered jailhouse communications indicating Gentile discussed making payments of $2.5 million or more to secure his clemency. Gentile served less than two weeks of his seven-year sentence.
events.why_relevant: Shutting down an investigation into potential corruption in the clemency process undermines rule of law and suggests use of presidential power for personal benefit or quid pro quo arrangements.
